aum.title: Assets under management (Eastspring)
aum.content:
AUM is the value of client assets Eastspring, Prudential's Asia/Africa asset manager, runs or administers — separate from the insurance balance sheet.

For Prudential plc: Eastspring's fee income scales with AUM, so this is the asset-management engine alongside the insurance new-business engine (APE/VNB below). Growth comes from net inflows and market performance, not underwriting.

What to watch:

  • Net flows versus market-driven AUM moves
  • Fee margin (revenue / average AUM) holding up as AUM grows

apeVnb.title: APE sales and Value of New Business (VNB)
apeVnb.content:
APE (Annual Premium Equivalent) is the standard insurance volume measure: regular new premiums plus 10% of single premiums, so a $10,000 single-pay policy and a $1,000/yr regular policy both count as $1,000 of APE. It answers "how much new business was sold," not "how much premium was collected."

VNB (Value of New Business) is the discounted profit that new APE is expected to generate over the life of the policies, net of the capital needed to write it. It is the insurer's forward-looking equivalent of a manufacturer's new-order margin.

For Prudential plc: the VNB/APE ratio (the "new business margin") is the number to track — Pan-Asia/Africa life insurers are valued on their ability to keep selling profitable new business, not on current-year premium income, which is why the CSV's Revenue line is a weak growth proxy for this company.

What to watch:

  • VNB margin (VNB / APE) rising or falling
  • APE growth versus VNB growth — growing sales at a falling margin is a warning sign
  • Only FY2024-FY2025 are disclosed on a comparable IFRS 17 basis in the filings extracted so far

embeddedValue.title: Embedded Value (EV)
embeddedValue.content:
Embedded Value is an actuarial net-asset-value measure specific to life insurers: shareholders' net assets plus the discounted present value of profits expected to emerge from policies already on the books (the "in-force" book), less the cost of holding required capital against them.

For Prudential plc: EV is the closest insurance-industry analogue to book value for a normal company, and EV growth (opening EV + VNB + operating experience/assumption changes + investment variance - dividends) is the insurer's equivalent of return on equity. It is also the basis management quotes per-share ($14.83/share at FY2025) when discussing intrinsic value.

What to watch:

  • EV growth rate versus the cost of equity used in the DCF
  • How much of the EV increase is VNB (new business, repeatable) versus one-off assumption or investment variance

balanceSheet.title: Balance sheet
balanceSheet.content:
Shareholders' equity is assets less liabilities; plotted against total liabilities to show leverage.

For Prudential plc: equity that grows only through revaluations or share issues is not the same as retained earnings.

What to watch:

  • Liabilities growing faster than equity
  • Goodwill share of equity after acquisitions

cashDebt.title: Cash and debt
cashDebt.content:
Cash & equivalents against total borrowings (leases excluded unless noted).

For Prudential plc: the DCF's net-debt bridge uses these balances at the latest balance-sheet date.

What to watch:

  • Net debt trend versus EBITDA
  • Refinancing dates and covenants in the filings

epsDps.title: EPS and dividends
epsDps.content:
EPS is net income per share; DPS is the cash dividend paid per share. Both are in major currency units.

For Prudential plc: the payout ratio (DPS / EPS) shows how much of earnings is returned versus reinvested.

What to watch:

  • EPS growth versus net income growth (dilution)
  • Dividends funded from earnings, not debt

fcf.title: Free cash flow
fcf.content:
Reported FCF is operating cash flow less capital expenditure. Owner FCF (from the DCF) further deducts stock-based compensation, interest income and lease principal -- the cash an owner could actually take out.

For Prudential plc: the gap between net income and owner FCF is the earnings-quality question the valuation is built on.

What to watch:

  • FCF persistently below net income
  • Working-capital swings inflating one year's FCF

ocfCapex.title: Operating cash flow and CapEx
ocfCapex.content:
Operating cash flow is cash generated by operations; CapEx is cash invested in fixed and intangible assets.

For Prudential plc: CapEx here is shown as stored (sign convention varies by ticker); the DCF splits it into stay-in-business and growth where disclosed.

What to watch:

  • CapEx rising faster than revenue
  • OCF that diverges from EBITDA

profit.title: Profit lines
profit.content:
Gross profit is revenue less cost of revenue; operating income deducts operating expenses; net income is after interest, tax and one-offs.

For Prudential plc: the three lines together show where margin is made and lost between the top line and the bottom.

What to watch:

  • Operating income growing slower than gross profit (opex creep)
  • Net income far from operating income (interest, tax, one-offs)

revenue.title: Revenue
revenue.content:
Revenue is the top line: what customers paid for goods and services in the period, before any costs.

For Prudential plc: the growth rate matters more than the level; compare it with the DCF's base-case growth path below.

What to watch:

  • Acceleration or deceleration in YoY growth
  • Whether growth is organic or acquired
  • Interim rows show seasonality

sbc.title: Stock-based compensation and share count
sbc.content:
Stock-based comp is the expense of equity awards; shares outstanding shows the dilution it causes net of buybacks.

For Prudential plc: the DCF charges SBC as a cash cost and holds the share count flat, so this chart is the check on that assumption.

What to watch:

  • Share count rising while buybacks are advertised
  • SBC as a percentage of revenue
